title: Fitting brick slip cladding to an interior wall
subtitle: Adhesive-fix thin brick slips to a plasterboard or masonry wall for an exposed brick effect
excerpt: How to fit brick slips to an interior wall using tile adhesive. Covers setting out, cutting slips, applying adhesive, grouting with mortar or grout, and sealing the finished surface.
sourceNotes: UK trade practice for decorative brick cladding. Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: A thin facing cut from a real brick or cast in reconstituted brick material, approximately 20 to 25 mm thick, used to clad a wall surface with the appearance of exposed brickwork. Brick slips are adhesive-fixed and grouted like large tiles.

The mortar or grout joint between individual bricks or brick slips. In brickwork the standard joint is 10 mm wide. The style and finish of the joint (flush, recessed, rounded) changes the character of the finished wall.

content.text: are thin brick facings, adhesive-fixed to a plastered or plasterboard wall to give the appearance of exposed brickwork without the structural weight. The job is set out in courses with a 10 mm
, fix with grey tile adhesive, and grout with a brick-effect mortar. A feature chimney breast or alcove back wall takes a full weekend.

Start by dry-laying a single course along the floor, spacing the slips 10 mm apart with tile spacers. Count the number of slips per row and calculate the cut at each end. Aim for a cut larger than half a slip at both ends; if the layout gives a small sliver at one end, offset the starting point by half a slip (a half-bond). Mark a horizontal level line at the height of the first course with a pencil and spirit level. This line is the foundation of every course above it.

The wall surface must be clean, dry, and free from loose paint or plaster. Plasterboard accepts tile adhesive directly if the paper face is undamaged. Skim-coated plasterboard or painted masonry must be primed with an SBR bonding agent or a dedicated primer recommended by the adhesive manufacturer. Allow the primer to dry fully before fixing slips.

Cut brick slips with an angle grinder fitted with a diamond blade, or a tile saw. Work outdoors or in a ventilated space and wear a dust mask and safety glasses. Brick slip cuts are never perfectly clean; slight irregularity at the joint edges adds to the handmade character. Cut all the pieces for one wall section before starting to fix, so you can see the full layout.

Apply grey flexible tile adhesive to the back of each slip with a filling knife (the buttering method), covering the full back face to a depth of about 5 mm. Press each slip firmly onto the wall, aligning the bottom edge with the level line. Use 10 mm tile spacers in the horizontal joints. Work in courses from the bottom upward. On plasterboard walls, do not fix more than two or three courses before allowing the adhesive to grip, or the weight of the slips may cause slippage.

Allow the adhesive to cure for at least 24 hours before grouting. Mix a ready-mixed brick mortar or a sand-and-cement grout to a stiff paste. Press the grout into the joints using a grout float or a pointing bag. Work it fully into the joints and remove the tile spacers as you go. Before the grout stiffens, drag a rounded stick or a dry brush along the joints to give a slightly recessed profile. Wipe the face of the slips clean with a damp sponge before the grout dries hard.

Leave the grout to cure for three to five days, then apply one coat of brick and masonry sealer using a brush. The sealer reduces dust and makes the surface easier to wipe clean. In a kitchen or behind a cooking area, use a heat-resistant silicone sealer. In a living area, a matt clear masonry sealer is the normal finish.
Stretcher bond (all slips running horizontally, each course offset by half) gives the classic English brick look. Stack bond (slips in a grid without offset) reads as a contemporary feature wall.
Reclaimed slips vary in thickness; sort slips into groups by thickness before fixing and keep the thicker ones to one section of the wall. Shim behind thinner slips with additional adhesive.

attrs.symptom: Slips sliding down the wall before adhesive grips
attrs.cause: Too much adhesive or fixing too many courses before allowing initial set. Heavy real-brick slips are heavier than ceramic tiles.
attrs.fix: Work in sections of four or five courses, then allow 30 to 60 minutes before continuing upward. Prop slips with temporary wedges at the bottom joint if slippage continues.

attrs.symptom: Grout lines uneven in width across the wall
attrs.cause: Slip thickness varies, or spacers were not used consistently.
attrs.fix: Use the same size spacer throughout. Accept minor variation as part of the handmade character of brick slip work.

attrs.symptom: Mortar efflorescence (white staining) appears on slip faces after a few weeks
attrs.cause: Soluble salts in the adhesive or grout migrating to the surface as moisture evaporates.
attrs.fix: Brush off with a stiff dry brush. Repeat if it returns. Seal the surface after the staining stops recurring, usually after two or three weeks.
